nodes.label: Permutations, Combinations and Combinatorics
nodes.note: Counting principles, permutations, combinations, distribution, and binomial expansions form the JEE combinatorics backbone. Almost every counting PYQ reduces to one structured case split.

nodes.label: Counting Principles
nodes.note: The sum and product rules plus complement arguments decide every direct count. Factorials supply the raw material.

nodes.label: Sum Rule
nodes.note: Mutually exclusive alternatives add: $$N = m + n$$. Use it for case splits like 'numbers divisible by 2 or 5'.

nodes.label: Product Rule
nodes.note: Sequential dependent stages multiply: $$N = m \times n \times p$$. Password and license-plate problems are direct applications.

nodes.label: Complement Principle
nodes.note: Count the unwanted arrangements and subtract: $$N_{wanted} = N_{total} - N_{unwanted}$$. Often the only clean route when 'at least one' appears.

nodes.label: Bijection Principle
nodes.note: A one-to-one correspondence transfers a count to a simpler set with the same cardinality. Classic use: mapping subsets to binary strings of length n, giving $2^n$.

nodes.label: Factorial Notation
nodes.note: $$n! = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 1, \ 0! = 1$$. Every arrangement count in this chapter is a quotient of factorials.

nodes.label: Permutations
nodes.note: Ordered selections from distinct or repeated objects.

nodes.label: Permutations of Distinct Objects
nodes.note: The number of ordered r-selections from n distinct objects is $${}^nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$. Arrangement of 5 students in a row is $5!$.

nodes.label: Arrangements with Repetition
nodes.note: With repetition allowed, each of the r positions has n choices: $$N = n^r$$. This counts strings of length r over an n-letter alphabet.

nodes.label: Example: PIN Codes
nodes.note: A 4-digit PIN with digits repeatable has $10^4 = 10000$ possibilities, direct product-rule reasoning.

nodes.label: Arrangement Constraints
nodes.note: Block (tie) method, gap method, and dictionary rank handle restricted arrangements.

nodes.label: Block Method
nodes.note: Glue the objects that must stay together into one super-object: $$N = k! \times (\text{internal arrangements})$$. For the word MOTHER with vowels together, treat OE as one block.

nodes.label: Gap Method
nodes.note: Arrange the free objects first, then place restricted ones in the gaps: $$N = (\text{free})! \times {}^{g}P_{r}$$. No two vowels together means vowels go into consonant gaps.

nodes.label: Lexicographic Rank
nodes.note: Rank a word in dictionary order by counting words starting with smaller letters at each position. Rank of a permutation like 'EAMCET' needs a left-to-right factorial count.

nodes.label: Example: Rank of a Word
nodes.note: For words from letters A, B, C with all used, words starting with A come first ($2! = 2$ of them); this prefix-counting logic gives the rank.

nodes.label: Combinations
nodes.note: Unordered selections and the identities that simplify them.

nodes.label: Combinations of Distinct Objects
nodes.note: Selecting r from n without regard to order: $${}^nC_r = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$$. Choosing a 3-member team from 10 players is ${}^{10}C_3 = 120$.

nodes.label: Pascal's Identity
nodes.note: $${}^nC_r = {}^{n-1}C_{r-1} + {}^{n-1}C_r$$ underlies Pascal's triangle. It justifies term counts in binomial expansions.

nodes.label: Multiset Selection
nodes.note: Selecting r objects from a set with repetitions allowed: $$N = {}^{n+r-1}C_{r}$$. Choosing 4 fruits from 3 types with repetition allowed gives ${}^{6}C_4 = 15$.

nodes.label: Symmetry of nCr
nodes.note: $${}^nC_r = {}^nC_{n-r}$$ because choosing r to include equals choosing n - r to exclude. It halves computation when r > n/2.

nodes.label: Circular and Identical Arrangements
nodes.note: Rotations merge in a circle; alike objects divide out permutations.

nodes.label: Circular Permutations
nodes.note: Fix one object to kill rotational duplicates: $$N = (n-1)!$$. The round-table seating of n people gives $(n-1)!$.

nodes.label: Garland (Necklace) Symmetry
nodes.note: Flipping a garland also duplicates arrangements, so divide by 2: $$N = \frac{(n-1)!}{2}$$. Distinguishing garlands from rings is a classic JEE MCQ twist.

nodes.label: Permutations of Multisets
nodes.note: With n_i alike objects of each type i, divide by the repeats: $$N = \frac{n!}{n_1!\, n_2! \cdots n_k!}$$. Arrangements of MISSISSIPPI follow this template.

nodes.label: Division and Distribution
nodes.note: Splitting distinct or identical objects into groups is stars-and-bars territory.

nodes.label: Division into Unequal Groups
nodes.note: Divide n distinct objects into groups of sizes $p, q, r$: $$N = \frac{n!}{p!\,q!\,r!}$$. Group labels matter only when groups are sized differently and destinations differ.

nodes.label: Division into Equal Groups
nodes.note: For k equal groups of size m, divide further by the group orderings: $$N = \frac{n!}{(m!)^k \, k!}$$. The extra $k!$ kills the interchange of identical groups.

nodes.label: Stars and Bars
nodes.note: Non-negative integer solutions to $x_1 + \dots + x_k = n$: $$N = {}^{n+k-1}C_{k-1}$$. Distributing identical chocolates to k children maps directly onto this count.

nodes.label: Positive Integer Solutions
nodes.note: Strictly positive solutions to $x_1 + \dots + x_k = n$ need $x_i \ge 1$: $$N = {}^{n-1}C_{k-1}$$. Substitute $y_i = x_i - 1$ and reuse stars and bars.

nodes.label: Advanced Combinatorics
nodes.note: PIE, derangements, surjections, and prime-exponent in factorials.

nodes.label: Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.note: Count a union by adding singles, subtracting pairs, adding triples: $$|A \cup B \cup C| = \sum |A_i| - \sum |A_i \cap A_j| + |A \cap B \cap C|$$. 'At least one' counts for properties use it.

nodes.label: Derangements
nodes.note: Permutations with no fixed point: $$D_n = n! \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$$. The !n notation (subfactorial) counts hat-check disasters and letter swapped envelopes.

nodes.label: Onto Functions (Surjections)
nodes.note: Number of onto maps from an m-set to an n-set: $$N = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k {}^nC_k \, (n-k)^m$$. Applying PIE to 'every element hit' gives this inclusion count.

nodes.label: Legendre's Formula
nodes.note: Exponent of a prime p in n!: $$E_p(n!) = \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^2} \right\rfloor + \cdots$$. It settles trailing-zero and divisibility questions about factorials.

nodes.label: Divisor Count from Factorization
nodes.note: If $N = p_1^{a_1} p_2^{a_2} \cdots$, then the number of divisors is $$\tau(N) = (a_1+1)(a_2+1)\cdots$$. Pairing divisors around $\sqrt{N}$ relates to product problems.

nodes.label: Binomial Theorem
nodes.note: Expansions, term analytics, and coefficient series - a guaranteed JEE Main presence.

nodes.label: General Expansion
nodes.note: $$(x + a)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} {}^nC_r x^{n-r} a^r$$. The $(r+1)$th term is ${}^nC_r x^{n-r} a^r$ and there are n + 1 terms total.

nodes.label: Middle Term
nodes.note: For even n the middle term index is $r = n/2$: $$T_{n/2 + 1} = {}^nC_{n/2} x^{n/2} a^{n/2}$$. For odd n there are two middle terms, $r = (n-1)/2$ and $(n+1)/2$.

nodes.label: Numerically Greatest Term
nodes.note: Find r from the ratio test on $|T_{r+1}/T_r|$ and the threshold $r \le \frac{(n+1)|a|}{|x| + |a|}$$. JEE traps students who forget the integer-floor boundary.

nodes.label: Binomial for Any Index
nodes.note: For any rational alpha with |x| < 1: $$(1+x)^\alpha = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-r+1)}{r!} x^r$$. Approximation $(1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ holds when $|x| \ll 1$.

nodes.label: Multinomial Theorem
nodes.note: $$(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n = \sum \frac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2! \cdots n_k!} x_1^{n_1} \cdots x_k^{n_k}$$. The number of distinct terms is ${}^{n+k-1}C_{k-1}$.
